<reason>PRO (Side B) built a cleaner, more decision-relevant case and defended it through the pressure. Its opening framed the motion as restoring a comparison the customer already believes they are making, and its Rebuttal 1 reframe — the "rival" is the restaurant whose food is already in the cart — substantially defused CON's strongest opening line (compelled cross-promotion / slippery slope). PRO's reading of "independent" as independent-of-the-app was a plausible reading of the motion and was delivered directly in A1 when CON pressed it. PRO also answered workability by pointing out apps already publish unaudited restaurant-entered prices, and turned CON's fee-relocation argument into a dilemma. CON (Side A) did real work: the feedback-loop distinction in A2 was a genuinely sharp point, and the loss-aversion answer in A1 was a legitimate response to PRO's dichotomy. But CON's core position — that showing a true, materially lower price to the customer is "friction engineered into someone else's checkout" — is hard for a third-party reader to accept, and PRO's closing exploited it effectively. CON's harms (fee relocation) stayed live but were weighed against a plausible rule that leaves the choice with the buyer, and CON never showed why the motion requires the audit it kept demanding. Clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [B2.1]-[B2.4] reframe that the "competitor" is the restaurant itself, not a stranger's till, which collapsed CON's compelled-cross-promotion and slippery-slope arguments; CON's Q1 tried to reopen it, but PRO's A1 reading of "independent" as independent-of-the-app held, and CON effectively abandoned the "rival" line thereafter.</best_rebuttal>
